name: Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL) Injury
summary: Partial or complete ACL disruption causing rotational and anterior knee instability, often during pivoting, deceleration or awkward landing.

redFlags: Locked knee suggesting displaced meniscal tear
Large acute effusion with severe pain requiring medical assessment

tests.name: Lachman Test
tests.positive: Increased anterior translation with a soft or absent endpoint compared with the other side.

tests.name: Anterior Drawer — Knee
tests.positive: Excess anterior tibial translation or soft endpoint.

tests.name: Pivot Shift
tests.purpose: Assess functional rotational instability associated with ACL deficiency.
tests.positive: A palpable clunk/shift as the lateral tibial plateau reduces.

stages.label: Acute Recovery / Prehabilitation
stages.goal: Settle effusion, restore extension, recover quadriceps activation and normal gait.
do: Shared orthopaedic decision-making for operative vs nonoperative pathway
dose: Quad sets: 5–10 x 5–10 s, several times/day
Straight-leg raise if no extension lag: 3 x 8–15
Stationary bike when ROM permits: 10–20 min low intensity

stages.label: Strength & Neuromuscular Control
stages.goal: Build quadriceps/hamstring strength and lower-limb control.
do: Closed- and open-chain knee strengthening as appropriate
dose: Knee extension within appropriate tolerated range: 3 x 8–15

stages.label: Running, Plyometrics & Return
stages.goal: Restore high-speed force, landing, cutting and sport capacity.
moveOn: Objective strength and hop symmetry appropriate for sport
Stable knee and satisfactory movement quality

returnCriteria: High quadriceps/hamstring strength relative to sport demands

structures: Possible associated meniscus, collateral ligament or osteochondral injury
mechanism: Non-contact pivot/cut with knee valgus and rotation
classification: Grade III complete tear; functional instability varies
investigations: MRI is commonly used to define ACL and associated injuries when indicated.
Radiographs may be required after trauma to exclude fracture.
manual: Patellofemoral/tibiofemoral mobilization may be used when joint mobility limits ROM.
Soft-tissue work can be an adjunct for short-term symptoms; it does not restore ligament stability.
Manual therapy should support, not replace, strength and neuromuscular rehabilitation.
modalities: NMES may be useful when substantial quadriceps activation failure exists, especially post-operative/early rehab.
Cryotherapy/compression can help symptom and effusion management.
Passive modalities should not replace progressive exercise.
mistakes: Using time alone for return to sport
Neglecting quadriceps strength and landing/cutting mechanics
pearls: A soft endpoint on Lachman after a pivot injury is a key ACL clue.
Rehabilitation quality matters whether the patient follows operative or nonoperative management.
Rapid substantial effusion after a pivot injury raises concern for significant intra-articular injury but is not specific to ACL rupture.
In an acutely painful, guarded knee, repeat examination after pain and swelling settle rather than forcing provocative tests.
Rehabilitation decisions should integrate instability episodes, activity goals, strength, movement quality and associated injuries—not MRI wording alone.
Before running, cutting or pivoting, assess progressive single-leg strength, landing control and sport-specific tolerance; time since injury alone is not clearance.

tests.name: Lachman Test
tests.positive: Increased anterior translation with a soft or absent endpoint compared with the other side.
tests.patientPosition: Supine; knee flexed about 20–30° with hamstrings relaxed.
tests.handPlacement: One hand stabilizes the distal femur; the other grasps the proximal tibia.
procedure: Translate the tibia anteriorly with a quick but controlled movement.
Assess amount of translation and endpoint.
tests.interpretation: Strongly supports ACL injury when consistent with mechanism and history.

tests.name: Anterior Drawer — Knee
tests.positive: Excess anterior tibial translation or soft endpoint.
tests.patientPosition: Supine; hip about 45°, knee 90°, foot stabilized.
tests.therapistPosition: Sitting or standing near the foot.
tests.handPlacement: Hands around proximal tibia with thumbs near the joint line.
tests.interpretation: Supports ACL insufficiency; can be less sensitive acutely due to guarding.

tests.name: Pivot Shift
tests.purpose: Assess functional rotational instability associated with ACL deficiency.
tests.positive: A palpable clunk/shift as the lateral tibial plateau reduces.
tests.handPlacement: One hand controls the heel/tibia; the other applies valgus force near the proximal tibia.
procedure: Apply internal tibial rotation and valgus stress.
Observe/feel for tibial reduction around early flexion.
tests.interpretation: Supports ACL-deficient rotational instability; best performed by experienced clinicians.

story.headline: A pop, a pivot and the knee that lost trust in itself
story.scene: A basketball player plants her foot, turns to pass and hears a pop. The knee swells quickly. By the next morning she says, 'The pain is calmer, so the ligament must be fixing itself, right?' The plot is not that simple.
story.dialogue: Patient: 'It's only painful when I try to turn.' Therapist: 'That's exactly why we care about the turning part.'
story.clue: Pivot mechanism, rapid effusion and instability raise suspicion for ACL injury, often with associated meniscal or cartilage damage. Lachman findings add clinical evidence but are not a solo verdict.
story.twist: A better pain score does not prove restored rotational control. Nor does every ACL injury require the same surgical path; shared decisions depend on associated injury and goals.
story.aha: The first big win is often full knee extension and quadriceps activation—not the fanciest balance drill on social media.
story.patientTranslation: One of the knee's important stabilizing ligaments may be injured. We will check for associated damage, help the swelling and motion settle, and plan strengthening with the appropriate specialist if needed.
story.clinicianReasoning: Check effusion, extension, neurovascular red flags and concomitant injuries. Combine Lachman and relevant tests with the history and imaging when indicated. Prehabilitation and later criteria-based strength, hop and psychological readiness guide return.
story.rehabBridge: Rebuild extension and quadriceps control first; then strength and single-leg mechanics; then running, deceleration, cutting and return-to-sport testing.
story.question: A pivot injury causes a pop, rapid swelling and a soft endpoint on Lachman. Which working hypothesis deserves priority?
options: ACL injury, with assessment for associated injury
story.explanation: The history and examination together strongly suggest ACL injury, but associated meniscal, collateral and osteochondral injury should also be assessed.
